{{short description|Triangle center}}

In [[Euclidean geometry]], the '''Apollonius point''' is a [[triangle center]] designated as ''X''(181) in [[Clark Kimberling]]'s [[Encyclopedia of Triangle Centers]] (ETC). It is defined as the point of [[Concurrent lines|concurrence]] of the three line segments joining each vertex of the triangle to the points of [[tangency]] formed by the opposing [[excircle]] and a larger circle that [[Problem of Apollonius|is tangent to all three excircles]].

In the literature, the term "''Apollonius points''" has  also been used to refer to the [[isodynamic point]]s of a triangle.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Katarzyna Wilczek|title=The harmonic center of a trilateral and the Apollonius point of a triangle|journal=Journal of Mathematics and Applications|year=2010|volume=32|pages=95–101}}</ref>  This usage could also be justified on the ground that the isodynamic points are related to the three [[Apollonius circle|Apollonian circles]] associated with a triangle.

The solution of the Apollonius problem has been known for centuries. But the Apollonius point was first noted in 1987.<ref name=evansville>{{cite web|last=Kimberling |first=Clark |title=Apollonius Point |url=http://faculty.evansville.edu/ck6/tcenters/recent/apollon.html |accessdate=16 May 2012 |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120510142037/http://faculty.evansville.edu/ck6/tcenters/recent/apollon.html |archivedate=10 May 2012 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=C. Kimberling|author2=Shiko Iwata |author3=Hidetosi Fukagawa |title=Problem 1091 and Solution|journal=[[Crux Mathematicorum]]|year=1987|volume=13|pages=217–218}}</ref>

==Definition==
[[File:Apollonius point.svg|thumb|280px|
{{legend-line|solid #333333|[[Extended side]]s of triangle {{math|△''ABC''}}}}
{{legend-line|solid blue|Excircles {{mvar|E{{sub|A}}, E{{sub|B}}, E{{sub|C}}}}}}
{{legend-line|solid green|Apollonius circle of {{math|△''ABC''}}}}
{{legend-line|solid red|Lines {{mvar|AA', BB', CC'}}: concur at the '''Apollonius point'''}}]]

The Apollonius point of a triangle is defined as follows.

:Let {{math|△''ABC''}} be any given triangle. Let the [[excircle]]s of {{math|△''ABC''}} opposite to the vertices {{mvar|A, B, C}} be {{mvar|E{{sub|A}}, E{{sub|B}}, E{{sub|C}}}} respectively. Let {{mvar|E}} be the circle which touches the three excircles {{mvar|E{{sub|A}}, E{{sub|B}}, E{{sub|C}}}} such that the three excircles are within {{mvar|E}}. Let {{mvar|A', B', C'}} be the points of contact of the circle {{mvar|E}} with the three excircles. The lines {{mvar|AA', BB', CC'}} are [[concurrent lines|concurrent]]. The point of concurrence is the ''Apollonius point'' of {{math|△''ABC''}}.

The Apollonius problem is the problem of constructing a circle tangent to three given circles in a plane. In general, there are eight circles touching three given circles. The circle {{mvar|E}} referred to in the above definition is one of these eight circles touching the three excircles of triangle {{math|△''ABC''}}. In [[Encyclopedia of Triangle Centers]] the circle {{mvar|E}} is the called the ''Apollonius circle'' of {{math|△''ABC''}}.

== Trilinear coordinates==
The [[trilinear coordinates]] of the Apollonius point are<ref name =evansville/>
<math display="block">
 \frac{a(b + c)^2}{b + c - a} : \frac{b(c + a)^2}{c + a - b} : \frac{c(a + b)^2}{a + b - c}
</math>
<math display="block">
 = \sin^2\! A \, \cos^2\! \frac{B - C}{2} : \sin^2\! B \, \cos^2\! \frac{C - A}{2} : \sin^2\! C \, \cos^2\! \frac{A - B}{2}.
</math>
